intro: Data analysts use SQL because it is the universal language for communicating with relational databases to extract and manipulate information. It remains the industry standard because it provides a precise, repeatable way to query data regardless of the underlying storage system, allowing analysts to bypass complex graphical interfaces.
tldr: SQL is the primary tool for querying relational databases.
Database interaction is often inefficient due to poor data quality and access silos.
Analysts waste nearly one-third of their day just trying to locate or access data.

blocks.text: The daily struggle of database interaction

You likely spend most of your day fighting with data structures rather than performing actual analysis. When you ask why do data analysts use SQL, the answer is simple. It is the most reliable way to get the data you need from a database. However, the process is rarely smooth. Databases are built for storage, not for your specific reporting needs. This mismatch forces you to write complex queries just to get a clean set of numbers.
Why database interaction is so slow

The primary cause of your frustration is technical debt. As companies grow, they add data to systems without a clear plan for how analysts will extract it later. You end up navigating massive, poorly documented schemas. You might need to join ten different tables just to answer a question that seems simple to a stakeholder. This is not a failure of your skill. It is a limitation of the infrastructure you are forced to work within.

items: Use a native Mac SQL client. Apps like TablePlus or DBeaver are much faster than web-based interfaces.
Standardize your queries. Keep a local library of snippets in a tool like VS Code to avoid rewriting the same joins.
Request read-only access to replicas. This prevents you from slowing down production databases when running heavy analytical queries.
Document your data definitions. If you find a column that is poorly named, save a mapping document so you do not have to guess next time.

faq.question: Is SQL still relevant for data analysts in 2026?
faq.answer: Yes. While AI tools can generate code, you still need to understand SQL to verify the output and handle complex database schemas.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur to write my SQL queries?
faq.answer: Lazur can help you draft code, but it does not execute queries against your database. Use it to explain syntax or debug your logic.
